This was... A very strange experience. Not in a bad way, mind you. I'll try to explain.

But first, have you heard of the Stanford prison experiment? If you have, you'll be in for a surprise. Anonymity, and the power to do act without repercussions. But in a way I didn't expect I would be able to experience in a game. This is very good. 

If you haven't, don't look it up. Just play the game, and don't worry about it.



Now that I got that weird comparison out of the way, here's what I want to say about this narrated, text-driven and heavily choice-based experience. You're not going to find many games like this one; it's unique and in a very well done way at that. In a dystopian but not far-fetched future that is dominated by public AND private surveillance, you're an investigator tasked with digging through the personal information of citizens of "The Nation", in the name of national safety above all else. While this is for the most part a linear game, you alone decide what information you upload to the Orwell Database, your employer. This means you alone have the power to decide what the public and the government knows about specific people.

So when you're assigned to an incident that shakes The Nation to its very core, you are the one who decides what happens next. And you're going to feel pretty strongly about it, one way or another.



This is a game that made me feel things I haven't before. Good things, bad things, and to be honest things about [i]me[/i] I weren't that aware of myself. Like I said, it was a strange experience.

I recommend this if you don't have anything against reading. You'll be doing that a lot. But it's definitely worth it.

Citizen science is the idea of having research conducted in organised form by non-professionals under the direction of scientific institutions. Some well-known examples of citizen science are found in astronomy and ornithology. In The Nation this philosophy has recently been extended into the realm of national security. Following the the Safety Bill that was initiated by The Party in 2012 the government of The Nation has received extended ability to observe the communication between its citizens in the name of national security. This has enabled the Orwell programme of surveillance, where Investigators have access to the communications of target persons and Advisors make recommendations for further actions. The similarities with citizen science is that the Investigators are just ordinary people from outside The Nation who look at the vast amounts of information and mark which data chunks that may be of interest. The Advisors, on the other hand, are professionals with experience and good contact with the legal authorities and they work with the provided data chunks. This system certainly ensures that not one single person gets too much power over the course of the investigations.

In Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You the player takes the role as a recently recruited Investigator. As a first case the player will have to look at a bomb that exploded at Freedom Plaza in central Bonton killing several citizens. A woman known to the police was seen at the scene and the player has to figure out whether she was involved in the terrorist attack.

The gameplay is straight-forward. It is just about using the Orwell interface to look at the data that are available and to decide what is relevant for the case at hand and what is not. It is fascinating to see how much of the interpretation of the available information depends on the context, meaning that the ordering of information has a big impact on the conclusions that are made. I liked the general idea of working with limited knowledge to understand a plot that is not straight-forward. The story itself makes sense, but it is only towards the end that I could see it so playing the game is like reading a good detective story with a possibility to make bad decisions which have effects on the outcome. Surprisingly for a detective story, Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also had a good replayability value, at least for me. I really had to see if it was possible to choose the bits of information I transferred in such way to make the best possible outcome, for the people involved, and for the citizens of The Nation as whole…

This is a truly amazing game. It really gets you thinking about mass surveillance. It's hardly impartial, but you get to see both the good and the bad aspects. If you have an interest in privacy, play this game. If you have never given it much thought, play this game. If you've ever said 'I have nothing to hide, it doesn't matter', play this game.

Pros:
- really gets you thinking about mass surveillance
- you control how the story unfolds based on what information you pass on to the government
- the story has some really great twists and surprises that I didn't see coming

Cons:
- Playing involves dragging and dropping pieces of information onto profiles of people you're investigating, but sometimes the drag and drop function is finicky, I occasionally had to retry multiple times to grab a piece of data. Not a big issue, but a minor annoyance.

A warning to achievement hunters: *do not* look at any 100% achievement guides before playing, they will ruin the story. You'll need 2 playthroughs anyway. Just play through normally the first time and you should be able to get all remaining achievements the second time.

Verdict: 10/10

You're a government operative of sorts investigating ongoing acts of terrorism in a fictional country only ever referred to as The Nation. This takes the form of mining people's websites, phone calls, text messages, etc looking for connections between various people of interests trying to build a case against the guilty and rule out the innocent. 

The actual gameplay boils down to reading through the various sources presented to you and pulling out highlighted text for presentation to the system so there's not a lot to it mechanically, but the story's well drawn and the characters are generally believable so you get pulled in pretty quickly. The subtleties generally come when you're presented with conflicting evidence and you need to decide what to mark as ignored and what to upload, as that will directly impact exactly how the people involved will get treated. 

I assumed it would go in hard on the 'surveillance is bad' angle but it as your character potentially instrumental in stopping people get murdered its position isn't as cut and dried as that. Ultimately you're playing a story with a few chances to influence it so if that's not your bag you won't enjoy it. If you're into that kind of thing though it's certainly a unique and interesting way of presenting a narrative (though it's entirely reading and clicking shit so your level of tolerance may vary).

I received Orwell from a friend who disagrees with the government monitoring its citizens, who was trying to make a point.

There's a demo that already tells quite a lot about this game. I'll just assume now that you've already played the demo and I will only go into details.

Episode 1 (the demo) is great: You have a target, you dig into her personal information, discover her personality, her social media accounts, her relations. You feel like digging into information you're not supposed to know, you're spying a stranger and soon feel like you know everything about him.

Sadly, Orwell can't keep quality this up. You're still wiretapping calls, crawling through social media accounts, gathering information and finding connections. However, the people aren't really the focus anymore - after episode 1, the story becomes more linear, you'll try to find out information about possible terrorist groups, but the game will just throw all the personal information at you while you're doing that. You don't really have to piece clues together, crawl through articles by yourself or solve riddles.

To summarize, Orwell simply feels like a visual novel that gives you a decision once in a while. Decisions, that - at least that's how they felt to me - barely have any impact. Few datachunks might lead to a different result, most don't, and some have to be uploaded so that the story progresses, even though they might seem misleading to you. However, the game doesn't give you the chance to dig deeper into those datachunks.

In the end, you'll be scrolling through new articles which the game throws at you, extracting 90% of the datachunks you find there to piece together the story while some guy comments every single of your actions. You'll do that for about 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you read the texts, and then the credits will roll.

Don't get me wrong - the story was exciting from beginning to the end, I enjoyed Orwell a lot, but it's way behind its potential. It gives the player almost 0 freedom and one might argue, whether or not this is intentional because of its setting.

If you regret one of your decisions, i.e. you accidentally uploaded a piece of information that you didn't want (which happened to me few times), bad luck. There's only autosave (it saves after every single decision) and you can't replay single chapters - even after finishing the game and can only start from scratch. There's not a lot replayability to it and the achievements are basically "don't upload a specific piece of optional information" which is kind of... meh. But it's the only thing this game offers and I can't imagine it being exciting anymore after you know the story.

If you like the setting, get it for a low price, enjoy it once, never touch it again. Then maybe look at the sequel (Ignorance is Strength) which improves on a few things (it actually gives you some freedom and you have to piece together some clues by yourself), but on the other hand tells a boring cliché story with uninteresting characters that ends after less than 3 hours.

It's so shame because episode 1 was so intriguing, but at least the demo shows you exactly what to expect from this game. If you enjoyed the demo and want more - go for it. If you didn't, skip the game - it won't become better after episode 1.

The user interface is quite crowded, given that a tool used to spy on civilians would be feature-filled, however navigating through the game's interface is not as fluid as you would imagine. The game is broken into 5 episodes which shift the focus towards different suspects around the same event with some humourous responses, should you decide to 'process' irrelevant information. Overall, this game and story is quite fun to follow and does keep you engaged around the concept of national surveillance. It explores the pros and cons of introducing such a system
